newsitem.title: UK: Boeing denies plans for futuristic superjumbo.
newsitem.headline: Boeing denies plans for futuristic superjumbo.

text.p: Boeing Co denied British newspaper reports on Friday suggesting that it has shelved plans to produce a bigger version of its own 747 jumbo jet to concentrate on developing a futuristic superjumbo with twice the capacity.

Reports in both The Times and The Independent speculated that Boeing had decided to focus instead on a futuristic 800-seat "giant flying wing" concept being developed by Boeing's prospective acquisition McDonnell Douglas (MDC).
"Speculation linking a McDonnell Douglas model airplane test programme with Boeing's decision to shelve its 747-X development announced this week is fanciful," said Boeing's local spokesman.
"The decision (to shelve the 747-X) was based on insufficient market demand to justify investment in an airplane larger than a 747," he said.

The Independent newspaper said MDC and Nasa are about to launch a test model of a triangular-shaped design at Stanford University in Connecticut and if successful two quarter-sized prototypes would be built for takeoff by the year 2000.
But the report said the aircraft would not be ready for flying passengers until 2010, with total development likely to cost up to $20 billion.

Boeing said earlier this week that it had shelved its 747-X project because too few airlines wanted to commit themselves yet and projected costs had more than doubled to $7.0 billion because airlines wanted almost a wholly new plane rather than a stretched version of the existing 747.
But Boeing is keeping a close watch on the progress of arch rival Airbus Industrie's proposals to produce an A3XX double-decker aircraft by 2003 with initial seating capacity of 550 passengers.

Industry sources said there was little doubt that Boeing was still working away behind the scenes developing both the 747X and all-new concepts for the larger aircraft which airlines say will be needed sooner or later to cope with the relentless climb in demand for air travel.
"If the market develops we will be ready," Boeing's spokesman said.
